newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl ally strikes back in Bonn pension row.
newsitem.headline: Kohl ally strikes back in Bonn pension row.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's powerful lieutenant Wolfgang Schaeuble delivered a stinging rebuff to Labour Minister Norbert Bluem on Thursday in a row over pensions reform which has caused a deep split in Kohl's party.
Bluem, Kohl's longest serving minister, clashed with the chancellor last month after producing a pensions reform scheme which ran counter to a government tax reform plan.

Bluem, who is often seen as the social conscience of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), appeared to win concessions in the pensions row, thus dampening speculation that he might deal a blow to the government by resigning.
But Schaeuble's attack, in an interview in the weekly Wirtschaftswoche, left no doubt that battle was being resumed.
"Clearly I have to be able to argue with Norbert Bluem about pensions reform without him immediately threatening to resign and triggering a wave of sympathy," he said.

Schaeuble rejected many of the key positions of Bluem and the experts who sat on his pension reform commission, charged with adjusting the pay-as-you-go state system to cope with the growing proportion of old people in the next century.
"The commission's report is only a basis for discussion," added Schaeuble, the influential parliamentary leader of the CDU and widely seen as Kohl's most likely successor.
Commission members had given the impression that the government had abandoned its plan to increase tax on pensions.
But Schaeuble said: "Nothing has been abandoned. The issue of tax on pensions isn't in the pension commission's brief."

The centre-right coalition government is determined to limit pensions contributions as a way to cut the burden of labour costs. But the question is a sensitive one for the CDU, which recruits a large share of its support from the older generation.
Bluem planned to take many non-pensions benefits out of the pension fund and instead finance them from taxes.
But Schaeuble said he preferred instead to raise higher pension payments from childless contributors who had not brought a new generation of contributors into the world.
He suggested raising the pension age from 2010 onwards, to keep pension contributions below 20 percent of earnings, instead of Bluem's idea of letting contributions rise to 23 percent.

Schaeuble also attacked the Free Democrats, junior partners in the coalition, for criticising the tax reform commission's proposal to tax life insurances. "We made that plan in agreement with the FDP," he said.
